sec.title: Background
sec.p: Stem cell donation (SCD) is essential to expanding donor pools for hematopoietic transplantation, yet the knowledge and educational needs of medical students remain insufficiently characterized. This study assessed medical students’ knowledge, attitudes, and behaviours regarding stem cell donation.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This cross-sectional study was conducted during the 2024–2025 academic year at the Faculty of Medicine, Gaziantep University (Turkey). A questionnaire assessed sociodemographic characteristics and SCD-related knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A total of 378 students (aged 18–34 years; 60.1% female) participated. Overall, 2.1% reported having donated stem cells and 38.9% intended to donate. 19% had received prior SCD training. The mean knowledge score was 14.67 ± 5.92 out of 27 (54.3%). Knowledge was higher among clinical-phase than preclinical students (p < 0.001), among those who had received training (p = 0.005), and among those willing to receive training (p = 0.009). Reluctance to donate was most often attributed to anticipated pain (20.6%) and concerns about adverse effects (13.8%); 47.9% would donate only to family members if needed.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Medical students demonstrated low-to-moderate knowledge with clear, teachable gaps. Integrating targeted early-phase modules and awareness activities into the curriculum may improve knowledge and willingness to donate, supporting donor recruitment efforts.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Clinical research indicates that hematopoietic stem cell transplantation may be an effective option in the management of more than 70 hematologic and immunologic disorders of varying etiology [1]. These treatments include the management of many life-threatening conditions such as leukemia, lymphoma, aplastic anemia, and inherited blood disorders [2]. Stem cell–based therapy is a modern treatment approach that utilizes the unique proliferative capacity of these cells and their ability to differentiate into various cell types, with the aim of regenerating damaged tissues or replacing them with new, healthy, and functional cells [3, 4].

According to the Worldwide Network for Blood and Marrow Transplantation (WBMT), approximately 1.5 million hematopoietic cell transplants were performed globally between 1957 and 2019. In 2018 alone, 93,105 procedures were reported worldwide, of which 48,680 were autologous and 44,425 were allogeneic transplants [5]. Current transplant volumes appear insufficient to meet global demand; it is estimated that 110,000–120,000 patients require transplantation each year [6]. In Turkey, the Turkish Stem Cell Coordination Center (TÜRKÖK) reported that, as of 2025, the number of active unrelated volunteer hematopoietic stem cell donor candidates reached 1,181,208, with 29,791 matches achieved [7].

These data underscore the vital importance of stem cell donation (SCD). Insufficient or incorrect public information—as well as fears and concerns related to the process—are among the key barriers to recruiting adequate numbers of donors [8]. Consequently, assessing the public’s knowledge, attitudes, and practices about stem cell donation is critical for expanding donor pools and improving access to treatment. Medical students, as future physicians, serve as reliable sources of information for patients and families regarding stem cell donation, play an important role in correcting misconceptions, and contribute to shaping public trust in donation systems through their professional authority. Although physicians do not routinely counsel healthy donors, their recommendations are known to significantly influence health-related decisions such as vaccination, blood donation, and organ donation. Therefore, evaluating medical students’ knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding stem cell donation is essential both to inform future clinical practice and to train health professionals who can play an active role in public education. This study aimed to determine medical students’ knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors concerning stem cell donation.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: This was a cross-sectional, descriptive study. Data were collected from students who volunteered and provided informed consent using a 39-item questionnaire administered either online or through face-to-face interviews.

sec.title: Participants
sec.p: The study population comprised students enrolled at the Faculty of Medicine, Gaziantep University, Turkey. Sample size (n = 325) was computed using a single-proportion formula with 95% confidence (Z = 1.96), expected proportion p = 0.50, margin of error d = 0.05, and a design effect of 1.0 (allowing for ~ 10% non-response). A total of 378 students who provided informed consent were included. Inclusion criteria were active enrolment in the medical program and provision of informed consent; surveys with missing outcome data were excluded from analyses.

Ethics approval was obtained from the Gaziantep University Ethics Committee (Decision No.: 2025/35, Date: 12 March 2025), and permission for data collection was granted by the Dean’s Office of Gaziantep University Hospital. The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Data collection took place between 15 March and 15 April 2025.

sec.title: Questionnaire
sec.p: The questionnaire was developed by the authors in Turkish following a comprehensive review of the relevant literature and alignment with the study objectives [8–10]. Item generation was guided by key domains identified in the literature, and items were drafted to cover sociodemographic characteristics and experiences, as well as knowledge, attitudes, and behaviours regarding stem cell donation. To support content validity, the draft instrument was reviewed by an expert panel (family medicine, hematology, and medical education) for relevance, clarity, and coverage; minor wording revisions were made based on their feedback. As the questionnaire was originally developed and administered in Turkish, no translation or back-translation procedures were required. No pilot testing was conducted prior to the main survey administration, which is acknowledged as a limitation.

The questionnaire was administered both online (via Google Forms) and face-to-face. To prevent duplicate entries, online submissions required institutional login and timestamp verification, while face-to-face surveys were logged using unique study IDs. The instrument was specifically designed for this study and has not been published elsewhere. The English version of the questionnaire is provided as a supplementary file (Supplementary File 1) and cited in the main text.The instrument comprised 39 items. The first Sect. (5 items) recorded sociodemographic characteristics (age, sex, year of study, marital status, religious belief). The second Sect. (6 items) asked whether the participant had donated blood or stem cells, whether anyone in their circle had undergone or needed a stem-cell transplant, whether the participant had received training on stem-cell donation, whether they wished to receive such training, and their sources of information on stem-cell donation.

The third Sect. (8 items) assessed attitudes and behaviors related to stem-cell donation (e.g., intention to donate; expectations about pain/adverse effects; donation for religious reasons; donating only to family members; viewing donation as a civic responsibility; whether paying donors would increase donation; and awareness of eligibility requirements).

The final Sect. (27 items) assessed knowledge. The first 8 items asked whether specific diseases are treated with stem-cell transplantation and used a dichotomous scale (“yes/no”): correct answers were scored 1, incorrect answers 0. The remaining 19 items covered age/eligibility for donation, stem-cell sources, donation methods/procedures, and potential complications, and were rated on a 3-point Likert scale (“disagree,” “unsure,” “agree”). For these items, correct responses (i.e., “agree” for true statements and “disagree” for false statements) were scored 1; “unsure” was scored 0. The total knowledge score ranged from 0 to 27.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Analyses were performed using SPSS version 22.0. Descriptive statistics included frequencies, means, and standard deviations. The Kolmogorov–Smirnov/Shapiro–Wilk tests were used to assess normality. Group comparisons employed the Student’s t test or Mann–Whitney U test for two groups and one-way ANOVA for three or more groups. A two-sided p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Internal consistency of the questionnaire was evaluated using Cronbach’s α and showed high reliability (α = 0.894).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: %) sesults A total of 151 (39.9tudents were male and 227 (60.1%) were female; the mean age was 21.94 ± 2.18 years (range: 18–34). Overall, 96 (25.4%) participants were in the 2nd year and 46 (12.2%) in the 4th year of medical school. Sociodemographic characteristics are presented in Table 1. Preclinical phase was defined as Years 1–3 and clinical phase as Years 4–6.

sec.title: Donation/training history and information sources
sec.p: Only 8 (2.1%) students reported having donated stem cells. 11 (2.9%) indicated that they or a family member had undergone—or currently needed—stem-cell transplantation. 72 (19.0%) had previously received training on stem-cell donation, while 254 (67.2%) expressed willingness to receive such training (Table 1). As information sources about stem-cell donation, students most frequently cited medical school coursework (n = 304; 80.4%), followed by the internet (n = 124; 32.8%), social media (n = 116; 30.7%), donation campaigns (n = 37; 9.8%), television/radio (n = 29; 7.7%), and family/friends (n = 28; 7.4%).

sec.title: Knowledge score
sec.p: The mean knowledge score on stem-cell donation was 14.67 ± 5.92 out of 27 (54.3%). Mean scores were 14.29 ± 6.02 for males and 14.92 ± 5.86 for females, with no significant difference (p = 0.314). Knowledge was lower in preclinical compared with clinical students (p < 0.001). Knowledge did not differ by religious belief (p = 0.598). Associations between sociodemographic variables and knowledge scores are summarized in Table 1.

p.italic: p values from appropriate two-group tests as specified in Methods (Student’s t test or Mann–Whitney U); for multi-level variables use one-way ANOVA as applicable

sec.p: Students who had previously donated stem cells had a mean knowledge score of 18.25 ± 5.77, versus 14.59 ± 5.91 among those who had not donated; this difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.085, Table 1). Students who had received training scored higher than those without training (16.30 ± 5.24 vs. 14.29 ± 6.02; p = 0.005). Those willing to receive training also scored higher than those not willing (15.27 ± 5.96 vs. 13.44 ± 5.67; p = 0.009). Knowledge did not differ between students with self/family history of HSCT/HSCT need (17.54 ± 5.22) and those without (14.58 ± 5.93; p = 0.103; Table 1).

sec.title: Attitudes and behaviors
sec.p: 147 (38.9%) students stated that they were considering stem-cell donation. Reasons for reluctance included anticipating pain (n = 78; 20.6%) and concerns about adverse health effects (e.g., anemia, musculoskeletal problems, infection; n = 52; 13.8%). 33 (8.7%) cited religious reasons for not donating (Beliefs such as concerns about the violation of bodily integrity, uncertainty regarding religious permissibility, fear of harm (self-harm), and fatalistic views). 181 (47.9%) would donate only to family members in case of need. 219 (57.9%) agreed that donation is a civic responsibility, and 207 (54.8%) believed paying donors would increase donation. Only 93 (24.6%) reported knowing the eligibility requirements for being a donor. Attitudes and behaviors are detailed in Table 2.

sec.title: Disease indications
sec.p: Conditions most commonly recognized as treated with stem-cell transplantation were leukemias (n = 348; 92.1%), bone marrow cancers (n = 305; 80.7%), and myelodysplastic syndromes (n = 256; 67.7%). Response distributions for disease indications appear in Table 3.

sec.p: With respect to specific concepts, 98 (25.9%) correctly answered that ABO blood-group compatibility is not required for stem-cell donation; 103 (27.2%) correctly recognized that, compared with peripheral blood stem-cell transplantation, bone marrow transplantation carries a similar risk of acute GVHD but a lower risk of chronic GVHD; and 113 (29.9%) correctly stated that GVHD does not occur in autologous transplants (Table 4).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this study, 2.1% of medical students reported having donated stem cells, while 38.9% stated an intention to donate in the future. Among Saudi medical students, 1.6% reported bone marrow donation and 2.9% reported peripheral blood stem cell donation [8]. Additionally, the proportion of individuals registered as potential bone marrow donors was reported to be 9% in Saudi Arabia and 52.3% in Poland [8, 11]. In Turkey, 89.1% of midwifery and nursing students stated they planned to become hematopoietic stem cell donors [12]. These findings indicate that actual stem cell donation rates among medical students remain low across countries despite substantially higher levels of intention or donor registration, highlighting a persistent gap between willingness and actual donation behavior.

In our study, 24.6% of participants were aware of the eligibility criteria for stem cell donors. Similarly, only 8% of first-year medical and law students reported having knowledge about transplantation procedures [13], and 19.2% of health sciences students stated that they knew what stem cell donation entails [14]. Consistent with our findings, these studies indicate insufficient knowledge levels among students, and multiple reports from different regions of Turkey highlight gaps in educational curricula regarding stem cell donation and transplantation.

In our sample, 19.0% of participants had received education on stem cell donation, whereas 67.2% expressed a desire to receive such education. Similarly, in Saudi Arabia, 14% of medical students reported having received education on stem cells, while 72.1% indicated a willingness to pursue advanced training [15]. In Poland, 55% of medical students expressed interest in attending university courses on this topic [11]. Thus, both our study and prior work show limited training exposure but high demand for education.

The leading information source in our cohort was medical school education (80.4%), followed by the internet (32.8%) and social media (30.7%). In Jordan, physicians most often cited the internet (52.9%), books (52.1%), and lectures (47.6%) [16]. Among health sciences students in Turkey, 60.6% of those informed about stem-cell donation cited online sources, and 53.8% cited school-based sources [14]. Unlike several reports, our students predominantly referenced formal medical education, which may reflect curricular content, cultural context, and access to digital resources. Strengthening curricula, updating course content, and integrating high-quality online materials may simultaneously raise knowledge and motivation to donate.

Our students’ mean knowledge score was 14.67 ± 5.92 (54.3%). In Saudi medical students, overall stem-cell knowledge of 38.8% has been reported [15]; another Saudi study found 37.4% knowledge regarding donor compatibility and 23.6% regarding the donation process [8]. In Jordan, physicians’ overall knowledge averaged 51.3% [16], whereas Polish medical students showed 64.9% knowledge regarding HSCT [11]. In China, 79% of practitioners and medical students had low or moderate knowledge [17]. Collectively, our findings and prior research indicate low-to-moderate knowledge levels, supporting the need for targeted educational programs integrated into curricula and complemented by campaigns that promote active student engagement, which may also improve donation rates.

We found no sex-based difference in knowledge (p = 0.314). Prior studies have reported higher knowledge in male physicians (Jordan) [16] or female medical students (Poland) [11]. Discrepancies likely reflect cultural, demographic, and educational factors.

Knowledge was significantly lower in preclinical than clinical students (p < 0.001), mirroring a Saudi study in which clinical-phase students outperformed preclinical peers (p < 0.001) [8]. Given the emphasis on basic sciences in preclinical years and patient care/case-based learning in clinical years, an increase in knowledge with training progression is expected. Additionally, in its fourth year (clinical phase), HSCT is formally introduced as part of hematology and oncology rotations. Our results reinforce that curricular progression supports knowledge gains in this domain. It should not be overlooked that the disproportionate representation of certain academic years may have affected the overall information estimates.

Knowledge did not differ between students who had and had not previously donated (p = 0.085), consistent with reports from Saudi Arabia [8]. This suggests that donation behavior is not solely knowledge-driven; personal motivation, social awareness, process accessibility, and individual attitudes likely play important roles. Hence, efforts to increase donation should couple education with motivational messaging and process facilitators.

Students who had received training scored higher than those without training (p = 0.005), and those willing to receive training scored higher than those unwilling (p = 0.009). Controlled educational interventions—e.g., among nursing students in Korea—have demonstrated significant knowledge gains post-training [18], as have course-based interventions among first-year medical and law students in Turkey [13]. These findings support integrating structured educational modules, seminars, and campaigns to elevate knowledge and foster positive attitudes toward donation.

Regarding barriers, 20.6% of students did not want to donate because of anticipated pain, and 13.8% cited concerns about adverse health effects (e.g., anemia, musculoskeletal problems, infection). Comparable concerns were reported among Polish university students (pain 21.5%, complications 16.6%) [11] and Saudi medical students (long-term side effects 48.7%, procedural pain 38.7%) [8]. While reasons are broadly similar across settings, their prevalence varies, likely due to cultural and educational contexts. These data highlight the importance of myth-targeted education and awareness campaigns, with clear information on safety, pain management, and potential side effects to reduce anxiety and improve participation.

In our study, 38.9% planned to donate, yet 47.9% would donate only to family members. In Poland, 98% of medical students would donate to a sibling or parent if needed [11]; in the United States, 72% of medical students were willing to donate to any patient, while 98% would donate for a family member [19]. In Saudi Arabia, 47.2% of the public were willing to donate to both relatives and non-relatives, 32.6% to relatives only, and 20.2% were unwilling [20]. Our findings align with this pattern: willingness is higher for family members, suggesting donation motivation is closely tied to emotional bonds. Campaigns emphasizing solidarity and altruism may help extend willingness beyond the family circle.

In our study, 57.9% of students stated that stem cell donation is a social responsibility that everyone should fulfill, while 54.8% reported that providing financial compensation to stem cell donors could increase donation rates. In contrast, a study conducted in Poland reported that 72.9% of participants believed that stem cell donation should not be encouraged through financial incentives [11]. Similarly, in the study by Switzer et al. [21], the intention to donate hematopoietic stem cells among potential donors was found to be positively associated with individuals’ perceived sense of social responsibility toward society. In Turkey, hematopoietic stem cell donation is voluntary and unpaid for healthy individuals aged 18–50 years, and direct medical costs are covered by the healthcare system. However, indirect costs related to the donation process, such as lost workdays, transportation, or childcare expenses, may not always be fully reimbursed. This may partly explain participants’ views that providing financial support to donors could increase donation rates. Therefore, perceptions of financial neutrality may influence attitudes toward donation.

Most students correctly identified HSCT indications (leukemias 92.1%, bone marrow cancers 80.7%, myelodysplastic syndromes 67.7%), exceeding rates in a Saudi community sample (70.6%) [20] likely reflecting our medical-student cohort.

Notably, 75.1% correctly recognized that blood samples are collected from donor candidates for infectious disease serology, ABO typing, and HLA tissue typing. Although student-level data on this specific item are limited, the majority-correct response in our sample suggests that donor assessment procedures are learned in line with WMDA standards [22]. Likewise, 74.3% correctly understood that positivity for HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, or syphilis precludes donation, consistent with WMDA and clinical guidelines [22]. Reports of lower knowledge on donor eligibility in Saudi Arabia [8] and the U.S [19]. may indicate that our higher awareness is related to TÜRKÖK/Turkish Red Crescent educational efforts and curricular emphasis.

66.7% correctly identified stem-cell types (adult, embryonic, iPSC), aligning with “moderate” knowledge levels reported among health students in Saudi Arabia (72.4% and 65.3%) [23, 24]. This pattern suggests that typology knowledge tends to cluster at a moderate level, varying with curriculum, measurement tools, and timing; early, focused modules may help consolidate this knowledge.

Only 25.9% correctly answered that ABO blood-group matching is not required for donation. The literature notes frequent confusion between blood group and HLA matching in donor eligibility [8, 14, 25]. Authoritative sources emphasize that allo-HSCT matching is HLA-based and that ABO incompatibility is generally clinically manageable [26]. Incorporating brief case-based modules highlighting “HLA ≠ blood group” may reduce such misconceptions.

Finally, 27.2% correctly recognized that bone marrow vs. peripheral blood transplantation carries a similar risk of acute GVHD but a lower risk of chronic GVHD with bone marrow, and 29.9% correctly noted that GVHD does not occur in autologous transplants. Although student-level evidence on these specific items is limited, the low correct rates likely reflect the comparative and nuanced nature of these topics [27, 28]. Given the clinical importance of GVHD, visual and case-based modules are recommended to reinforce these concepts.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: This study has several limitations. First, its cross-sectional, single-institution design limits causal inference and generalizability beyond similar settings. Second, data were self-reported and may be influenced by selection and social desirability biases. Third, although the questionnaire was developed from prior literature, external validation was limited, and item-level misclassification is possible. Fourth, we used convenience sampling during a defined time window; nonresponse bias cannot be excluded. Fifth, convenience sampling limits generalizability beyond similar educational contexts. Sixth, no pilot testing was conducted, which has been acknowledged as a limitation. Finally, we did not assess longer-term knowledge retention or actual donor registration/behavior, so intention–behavior gaps may persist.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: These findings indicate a clear need for targeted educational interventions to increase awareness and participation in stem-cell donation among medical students. We recommend strengthening medical curricula with content that explicitly covers stem-cell donation, hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, and donor eligibility/processes; complementing this with student-led awareness campaigns, seminars, and volunteer donor information activities. In addition, experiential learning—for example, field placements and structured collaboration with bone marrow donor centers/registries—may foster students’ active engagement in the donation pathway.

Enhancing the knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors of medical students—tomorrow’s health professionals—will not only help raise donation rates but also counter misconceptions and increase public awareness around stem-cell donation. In the longer term, such initiatives are expected to expand the donor pool and thereby increase the life-saving potential of transplantation in hematologic diseases.
